title: The Same Mark, Two Different Distributions
scopeNote: This is the first experiment of the original, narrowed to the point that a raw score is not interpretable on its own. The second experiment placing one mark on two distributions at once, the extended treatment of one-tailed against two-tailed areas, and the read-the-curve challenge set stay in the longer version, and the page says so.
summary: A normal curve whose mean and spread the learner controls, drawn on a score axis that never moves, with the same axis relabelled in standard deviations directly beneath it. A mark stays where it is while the distribution slides underneath, and its z-score, percentile and tail areas change completely.
learningObjectives: State what the mean and the standard deviation each do to a normal curve.
Compute a z-score and read the percentile and tail areas that go with it.
Explain why the same raw score can be ordinary in one distribution and remarkable in another.
Explain why standardising relabels the axis rather than changing the distribution.
Explain why the 68, 95 and 99.7 figures are properties of the normal model rather than of data.
interactionTypes: three live controls over the distribution and the mark
a normal curve on permanently fixed score and density axes
a second axis showing the same scale relabelled in standard deviations
shaded area below the mark, updating live
a three-part challenge that sets the controls and names what to watch
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Everything is computed in the browser and is gone when the page is closed.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with every control a native range input carrying a live value output. The figure carries a description giving the mean, the spread, the mark, its distance from the mean in standard deviations and both tail areas, so no conclusion depends on reading the curve. The mark is distinguished from the mean by position, weight and an explicit on-figure label rather than by colour alone, and both labels are drawn with a background-coloured halo so they stay legible over the curve. The figure scrolls sideways rather than shrinking below legible label sizes on a narrow screen, and becomes a keyboard-reachable region when it does. Every change is announced through a polite live region. No timed content and no motion.
dataStatus: Illustrative. There is no dataset and no sampling: the curve is a normal density function drawn from the mean and standard deviation on screen. The marks and cohorts described are fictional, and no figure is a norm or a grade boundary.
simulationNotes: There is no randomness to seed. Percentiles and tail areas come from the normal cumulative distribution using the Abramowitz and Stegun 26.2.17 rational approximation. Both axes are deliberately fixed: the score axis always runs 0 to 100 and the density axis always to 0.105, which is just above the peak of the tightest curve the controls allow. If the axes rescaled to fit, every curve would look identical and the activity would demonstrate nothing. Fixing them is also what makes the falling peak visible as the spread widens, which is the conservation of total area made concrete. Very small tail areas are reported as a bound, below 0.1 per cent, rather than as a spuriously precise figure.
readmeTopic: why a raw score means nothing on its own, and what standardising actually does to the axis
